title: The history of radio
tagline: From a set of equations in 1865 to a voice from the sky in almost every Indian home.
intro: In 1865 James Clerk Maxwell predicted waves of electric and magnetic field that no one had seen. Within forty years, Hertz had made them, Jagadish Chandra Bose had sent them through walls in Calcutta, and Marconi had sent them across the Atlantic. Then came voices, tuning and the superhet, and after 1954 the cheap transistor set. In India, radio clubs in the 1920s grew into All India Radio, Akashvani, which now reaches almost everyone and still carries cyclone warnings to boats at sea.

eras.name: Invisible waves
eras.summary: Maxwell predicts electromagnetic waves, Hertz makes them, and Bose, Popov and Marconi learn to detect them and send signals.

eras.name: Voices on the air
eras.summary: Continuous waves carry speech and music, valves amplify them, and the superhet and FM make radios sharp and clear.

eras.name: Radio comes to India
eras.summary: Amateurs and radio clubs start broadcasting, the state takes over, and All India Radio becomes Akashvani, the voice of a new nation.

eras.name: A radio in every home
eras.summary: The transistor shrinks the radio into a cheap battery set, and India drops its radio licence.

eras.name: FM, communities and digital
eras.summary: FM, private stations, community radio, ham operators in disasters and digital radio bring new voices to the air.

events.title: Maxwell predicts electromagnetic waves
events.text: Maxwell read his paper 'A Dynamical Theory of the Electromagnetic Field' to the Royal Society in December 1864, and it was published in 1865. His equations said that electric and magnetic fields could travel together as a wave, at the speed of light.
events.why: It predicted radio waves, and showed that light is one of them.

events.title: Hertz makes and detects radio waves
events.text: Hertz made sparks jump across a gap in a metal dipole and caught the waves with a loop of wire that sparked in reply, across the room. He measured their wavelength and showed they reflect and refract like light.
events.why: Maxwell's invisible waves were real. The unit of frequency, the hertz, is named after him.

events.title: Bose sends millimetre waves through walls in Calcutta
events.text: At Presidency College, Bose built apparatus for waves only millimetres to centimetres long, far shorter than anyone else used. In a public demonstration in Calcutta, reported as November 1895, his waves passed through walls and a person to ring a bell and fire a small charge some 23 m away.
events.why: It was pioneering millimetre-wave work, now marked as an IEEE Milestone.

events.title: Popov's lightning detector
events.text: Popov showed a receiver with a coherer, a bell and a long wire antenna that rang when distant sparks or lightning sent out radio waves. Russia still celebrates 7 May as Radio Day.
events.why: Several inventors were closing in on wireless at the same time.

events.title: Marconi signals across his father's estate
events.text: Marconi found that raising his antenna higher and earthing his transmitter and receiver pushed the range of his spark signals from metres to kilometres, even beyond a hill.
events.why: Tall antennas and an earth connection made long-distance wireless practical.

events.title: Bose's iron-mercury-iron coherer
events.text: Bose described a detector with a drop of mercury between iron electrodes, listened to with a telephone earpiece, that did not need tapping to reset. Historians still debate how closely it matches the 'Italian Navy coherer' Marconi used in 1901.
events.why: It was an early self-restoring detector, and part of a long argument over credit.

events.title: A signal crosses the Atlantic
events.where: Poldhu, England, to St John's, Newfoundland
events.text: Using an antenna held up by a kite in Newfoundland, Marconi reported hearing the Morse letter S sent from Poldhu in Cornwall, about 3,500 km away. The waves had followed the curve of the Earth, bent back by the upper air.
events.why: Radio could span oceans. Marconi shared the 1909 Nobel Prize in Physics.

events.title: The first valve: Fleming's diode
events.text: Fleming patented a vacuum tube with a hot filament and a plate that let current flow one way only. It could detect radio signals far more reliably than a coherer.
events.why: The valve began electronics; its triode cousin could amplify.

events.title: Fessenden's Christmas Eve broadcast
events.text: Fessenden had already sent speech by radio in 1900. He later said that on Christmas Eve 1906 he broadcast music and a Bible reading to ships at sea using a high-frequency alternator. Historians question the details, because his account came 26 years later.
events.why: Continuous waves, modulated by sound, turned wireless telegraphy into radio broadcasting.

events.title: The crystal detector
events.who: Greenleaf Whittier Pickard, after J. C. Bose
events.text: Pickard patented a silicon crystal touched by a fine wire, the 'cat's whisker', as a radio detector. Bose had used galena crystals to detect waves in the 1890s and patented a crystal detector in 1904. Cheap crystal sets let millions listen with no battery.
events.why: The first semiconductor devices were radio detectors.

events.title: The superheterodyne
events.text: Serving in France in the First World War, Armstrong worked out how to mix an incoming signal with a local oscillator to shift it to a fixed, lower frequency, where it could be filtered and amplified easily. Lucien Lévy in France and Walter Schottky in Germany filed related ideas at about the same time.
events.why: Nearly every radio since the 1930s has been a superhet.

events.title: Scheduled broadcasting begins
events.text: KDKA went on air with the results of the US presidential election, and kept a daily schedule afterwards. It is widely called the first commercial broadcasting station, though others have rival claims.
events.why: Radio became something families listened to at home.

events.title: India's first licensed radio amateur
events.text: Gooptu is recorded as India's first licensed amateur radio operator. By the mid-1930s there were only about 20 in the country.
events.why: Hams were India's first radio makers, and later its disaster volunteers.

events.title: The Radio Club of Bombay goes on air
events.text: Radio broadcasting in India began with programmes from the Radio Club of Bombay and other clubs in Calcutta and Madras. Only a handful of people owned receivers.
events.why: It was the start of broadcasting in India.

events.title: The Indian Broadcasting Company
events.text: A private company opened stations in Bombay on 23 July 1927 and Calcutta on 26 August 1927. It went into liquidation in March 1930, and the government took over as the Indian State Broadcasting Service on 1 April 1930.
events.why: India's first regular stations, and the start of state broadcasting.

events.title: A licence to listen
events.text: Radio owners had to buy a yearly broadcast receiver licence from the post office. In the 1970s and early 80s it cost about ₹15 a year, and inspectors could check homes and shops for it.
events.why: For over fifty years, listening to the radio needed a permit.

events.title: Armstrong patents wideband FM
events.text: Armstrong received five patents for frequency modulation with a wide swing, which he showed could beat static far better than AM. He tested it from the Empire State Building in 1934–35.
events.why: FM gave radio its clear, static-free sound.

events.title: All India Radio is born, and so is 'Akashvani'
events.who: Indian State Broadcasting Service; M. V. Gopalaswamy
events.text: The state service was renamed All India Radio. The same year in Mysore, M. V. Gopalaswamy started a private station at his home and called it Akashvani, 'voice from the sky', a name suggested by the scholar Rallapalli Ananta Krishna Sharma. AIR adopted Akashvani as its on-air name in 1956.
events.why: It gave India its national broadcaster and its best-loved name.

events.title: Gandhi's only radio visit
events.text: Unable to travel to the Partition refugee camp at Kurukshetra, Gandhi went to All India Radio and spoke to the refugees over the air, on Diwali. At independence that year AIR had just six stations. India marks 12 November as Public Service Broadcasting Day.
events.why: Radio could reach people when a leader could not.

events.title: The transistor
events.who: John Bardeen, Walter Brattain and William Shockley
events.text: The point-contact transistor, a small piece of germanium that could amplify, was demonstrated at Bell Labs. Its inventors shared the 1956 Nobel Prize in Physics.
events.why: It made radios small, cheap and battery-powered.

events.title: Binaca Geetmala on Radio Ceylon
events.text: With film songs scarce on AIR in the early 1950s, Radio Ceylon's shortwave Hindi service drew huge Indian audiences. Ameen Sayani's weekly countdown of film songs, Binaca Geetmala, became a national habit.
events.why: It showed the hunger for film music that Vividh Bharati was built to meet.

events.title: The first transistor radio on sale
events.text: The Regency TR-1 was announced on 18 October 1954 and went on sale in November for US$49.95. It had four transistors and ran on a 22.5 V battery. Sony's smaller TR-63 followed in 1957 and made pocket radios a worldwide hit.
events.why: Radio left the living room and went everywhere.

events.title: Vividh Bharati
events.text: AIR launched Vividh Bharati, a service of film songs and light entertainment, partly to win listeners back from Radio Ceylon. It became one of India's most popular channels.
events.why: Film songs on the national radio shaped decades of Indian popular culture.

events.title: FM broadcasting starts in India
events.text: India's first FM broadcasts began in Madras, fifty years to the day after the Indian Broadcasting Company opened in Bombay.
events.why: FM brought clearer sound to Indian cities.

events.title: The radio licence is scrapped
events.text: India dropped the broadcast receiver licence for radio sets in the mid-1980s. Wikipedia gives 1984; some accounts say 1985. Listening became free for everyone.
events.why: The cheapest mass medium became free to use.

events.title: India's first private FM station
events.text: After the government auctioned FM licences, Radio City in Bangalore became the first private FM station on air. Many more followed in later phases. FMClear tells that story.
events.why: Private FM added dozens of new voices in each city.

events.title: India's first community radio: Anna FM
events.text: Anna FM, run from Anna University, became India's first community radio station, a small, low-power station serving its neighbourhood.
events.why: Radio could be run by and for a community.

events.title: Hams keep the Andamans talking after the tsunami
events.text: A ham radio DXpedition led by Bharathi Prasad was on the air in Port Blair when the earthquake and tsunami struck. With phone links down, the team relayed emergency and welfare messages to the mainland for days.
events.why: Radio that needs no towers works when everything else fails.

events.title: Community radio opens to NGOs
events.text: A new policy let non-profit groups, NGOs and agricultural universities, not only colleges, run community stations of up to 100 watts from masts up to 30 m high, covering about 12 km.
events.why: Villages got their own stations, in their own languages.

events.title: Mann Ki Baat
events.who: Prime Minister Narendra Modi, on All India Radio
events.text: The Prime Minister's radio talk began on AIR and has gone out roughly once a month since, carried across AIR's network and relayed by many other channels.
events.why: A sign of radio's reach in India in the internet age.

people.name: James Clerk Maxwell
people.note: Wrote the equations that predicted radio waves.

people.name: Heinrich Hertz
people.note: First to make and detect radio waves on purpose.

people.name: Jagadish Chandra Bose
people.note: Pioneered millimetre waves and crystal detectors, and patented very little of his work.

people.name: Guglielmo Marconi
people.note: Turned wireless into a worldwide business and shared the 1909 Nobel Prize.

people.name: Reginald Fessenden
people.note: Sent the first speech by radio and championed continuous waves.

people.name: Edwin Howard Armstrong
people.note: Invented the regenerative circuit, the superhet and wideband FM.

people.name: Ameen Sayani
people.note: His Binaca Geetmala countdown made him the best-known voice on Indian radio.

people.name: Bharathi Prasad
people.note: Led the Andaman DXpedition that became a lifeline after the 2004 tsunami.

series.title: Community radio stations on air in India
series.caption: From one campus station in 2004, community radio grew slowly, then quickly after the rules were eased.

facts: A medium-wave station at 1,000 kHz sends waves 300 metres long, as tall as a 100-storey tower.
AIR's medium-wave stations sit 9 kHz apart, and India's FM band runs from 88 to 108 MHz.
A crystal set has no battery: every bit of power you hear comes from the radio wave itself.
FM radios use a 10.7 MHz intermediate frequency so that no FM station's 'image' can land inside the band.
India marks 12 November as Public Service Broadcasting Day, for Gandhi's only visit to All India Radio.
